intro: Lesson 102: Data skills: tables, graphs and evaluation. Answer every question. Show your working. Mark it with the mark scheme and log any errors in your repair list.

questions.a: C) 52. 52 s is far from the other 0.6 mol/dm³ result (30 s) and breaks the trend.

questions.q: Mean of 12, 14, 13 and 25 (25 is an anomaly)?
Which axis for the independent variable?

questions.a: Change in y ÷ change in x

questions.q: A result that does not fit the pattern is...
Big question: how can you tell whether a conclusion is supported?
questions.a: Check the trend is clear across the range, repeats agree, anomalies are dealt with, and the science explains it.

questions.q: Calculate the mean at 0.6 mol/dm³ excluding the anomaly.
questions.model: Identify the anomaly: 52 s. Exclude it. Only 30 s remains (a third repeat would be needed), so mean = 30 s.

questions.q: Explain the trend using collision theory.
questions.a: Higher concentration: more particles in the same volume (1), more frequent successful collisions so faster reaction (1).

questions.q: A thermometer reads to 1 °C. What is its resolution?
Plot the mean data (portal graph grid), draw a curve of best fit, describe the trend and identify the anomaly.
questions.a: Axes labelled with units (1); scale over half grid (1); points correct (1); smooth curve (1); trend: time decreases as concentration increases (1); 52 s anomaly identified (1).
questions.model: Teacher draws the axes first: x: concentration (mol/dm³), 0 to 1.0; y: mean time (s), 0 to 100; plots the first point (0.2, 86).

questions.q: Calculate rate as 1000 ÷ mean time at 0.4 and 0.8 mol/dm³. What happens when concentration doubles?
questions.a: 22.7 and 43.5 s⁻¹ (1); the rate roughly doubles (1).

questions.q: Evaluate the conclusion 'Doubling concentration always doubles the rate'.
questions.a: Data roughly support it for this range (1); only two repeats, one anomaly (1); cannot extend beyond 0.8 mol/dm³ or other temperatures (1).
